utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Today, we have a quite unusual scheduling of our hearing, due to problems with courtrooms this morning, and another Chamber needed this courtroom for the first session, so that we start with a certain delay. Yesterday, Mr. Tolimir, I asked you, at the end of our hearing, do you have any estimation about the time you need with this witness. Do you have now any indication, for planning purposes? And, again, I don't want to put any pressure on you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May God's peace reign in this house, and may God's will be done in these proceedings and not necessarily mine. Your Honours, if the witness does not take up more than 50 or 60 per cent of the time, then we will finish today. But if he does, if he takes up more than 60 per cent of the overall time, we'll not be able to finish today, despite our fondest wish to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. While the witness is being brought in, just a housekeeping matter with respect to translations which are now up-loaded. We can advise the Court that the following exhibits have been up-loaded with translations: P766B, P804, P836A, P849, P852, and P987.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. These exhibits will now be admitted into evidence. Good morning, sir. Welcome back to the courtroom. We have a slight change of hearing time today, due to other matters. May I remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies, and Mr. Tolimir has some more questions for you. Mr. Tolimir asks you to be as short as possible in your answers, but as precise as possible. I know this is not very easy, but I think, due to the Court time for Mr. Tolimir, we all should take measures to be as precise and as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to welcome the witness. Please bear in mind what the Presiding Judge has told you. I'll do the same. We'll now follow your statement, which contains 14 pages. And in it, you said what you know and what you meant. I'll have questions for you. Please do not expand, because I may have questions to cover exactly what you want to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness's statement please be brought up in e-court. 5992 is the document number. Thank you. We can now see it. And could the Court please produce page 2 in the Serbian language, paragraph 3, line 3 -- page 2 paragraph 3, line 3, in Serbian. It's page 4 in English in e-court. This is what my Legal Adviser has just told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said this, and I'm reading from line 3: "The food convoys of the UNHCR did not always receive permit to pass through, but even when they did, lots of the food-stuffs would be seized by the VRS at Bratunac." Based on what you have stated, I would like to ask you the following: Do you remember, when was it that the VRS seized goods, and did anybody bother to write a protest to the Main Staff in respect of such an event?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, my statement here is very correct, in that UNHCR convoys were being robbed, and that that is by the BSA, and we used to report about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If this completes your answer, could you please tell us: Why did VRS seize convoys in Bratunac, and whose convoys were those, and who were they intended for? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UNHCR convoys were for food and some non-food items meant for the residents of the enclave; that is, the Muslims who were living inside there. Yes, they were refugees in their own country.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at D70.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document to be displayed, could you please tell me whether those convoys ever brought food for the Muslim army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I knew, there is no food that was meant for the Muslim army. The food was all meant for the residents of Srebrenica who were displaced and who had no other source of income or even food.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether the DutchBat ever provided food to the BiH army, or any other necessities that were supplied by means of humanitarian convoys? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce D70. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think General Tolimir may be wanting D80, not D70, if I've got the document in mind. I think we were just showing a statement from General Nicolai. I don't know if that's the statement he wants to show, but I suspect it may not be. If it is, I'll sit down. But I think it may be D80. D70 wasn't on our list, but D80 was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's then look at D80. And I would like to thank Mr. Thayer for his assistance, although I'm not looking for a document signed by Mr. Nicolai. I'm looking for something else. In any case, this is the document that I wanted to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is, indeed, D80.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm going to read what I need to read. This is a document which was sent by the department in Srebrenica municipality. It was the Defence Secretariat, and its chief was Professor Suljo Hasanovic. Let's first ask the witness whether he knows who Suljo Hasanovic was and who -- and whether that person discharged the duties of the chief of the Defence Sector while he was deployed in Srebrenica. Just yes or no. Thank you. Can you tell us if you know this gentleman, Suljo Hasanovic, who was the secretary of defence in the municipality of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't remember this person very well. I don't remember knowing him, but my memory could be failing me. But also, the letter in question, I've never seen it. It's the first time I'm seeing it. And if it is from -- I can see it's from Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Federation of Bosnia, Defence Ministry, but then this -- if it is from the Muslim military to their headquarters, really, I'm not privy to what information is therein, nor was I supposed to know these things, because I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not accusing you of anything. I'm just asking you whether you know him or not. I'm happy with your answer. Thank you very much. I understand that you never saw the man. I'm not blaming you for that. I'm just asking you whether you knew him. Since you think that this was sent from Bosnia-Herzegovina, look at line 5, where it says "Department in Srebrenica municipality." And then it says "Srebrenica," and then there, a number, and again "Srebrenica, 5th of June, 1995." Were you in the enclave on that date, on the 5th of June, 1995? Just briefly answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And here you can see that he is sending this to Tuzla: "We hereby submit a list of the quantities of food, materiel, and technical equipment, and fuel issued to our military units in our area for the month of May 1995." And what follows is a list of things that the military units received; 25.900 kilograms of flour; 596 kilograms of sugar; 1.423 litres of cooking oil --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The poor interpreters. If you're reading from a document, you should slow down. It's impossible to translate that. It's really impossible. Please slow down. And continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In other words, he's submitting an overview of the quantities of food, materiel, and technical equipment, as well as fuel, that were issued to the military units in the area for the month of May 1995: 25.900 kilos of flour; 596 kilos of sugar; 1.423 litres of cooking oil; 619 kilograms of salt; 5.000 kilos of beans; 17.020 pieces of cold cuts; and so on and so forth. Tinned food, and the rest. I don't want to go on reading. I'll skip until the last line, where it says: "Some of the food was obtained from the Dutch Battalion." And above that, you can see that it says: "We wish to note that the above quantities have been separated out of the humanitarian aid contingent which arrived in the area through UNHCR ..." And now I would quote word for word: "We wish to know that the above quantities have been separated out of the humanitarian aid contingent which arrived in the area through UNHCR, while some of the food was obtained from the Dutch Battalion. "Until our ultimate victory!" Chief of Defence Sector, Suljo Hasanovic. Thank you. And now my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to give you some guidance. This is not appropriate use of time. Everybody can see the document in B/C/S and in English. Then you are reading it, then you are quoting from it, and then you are repeating some parts of the content of this document. If you want to speed up your examination, the witness can see that, and it's not necessary to put it twice on the record. Please be, yourself, a little bit more careful with time. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, could you answer briefly, bearing in mind the words that I just heard from the President. Does it transpire from the document that the BiH army in Bosnia-Herzegovina was provided food by the Dutch Battalion? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, my interpretation is not that way. The -- the kind of food we are talking about here, the supplies from UNHCR, and they are cited, are not -- were not meant for the Muslims' army. It's only that they're saying they separated the humanitarian aid. So they removed and -- you know, the aid and put it, like, is their supplies. That's my interpretation of the whole thing. And that can happen, because the supplies were coming to the stores in Srebrenica. If the authorities, that is, the opstina, if they vote it is better, instead of giving those it was meant for, and they take it for their own use, as a military, really we had not much control over that. Secondly, I don't think the Dutch Battalion were bringing supplies for the Muslim Army. So officially, me, as far as I know, there was nothing like that, that they would supply the Muslim Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, did you know where that warehouse was, the warehouse where humanitarian aid was off-loaded?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever carry out any checks, or controls, or an inspection as to who the recipients of the humanitarian aid were?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we used to go there when they were giving out the supplies to the locals. We used to go there, in most cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When were the supplies provided to the army, since you couldn't see it? Do you know how were the troops supplied? Because I can tell from this document that they were. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never witnessed any supplies being given to the military at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, can everything listed in this document arrive in one convoy?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that calls for a bit of a calculation, because one convoy is not one vehicle and convoys differ in terms of the supplies they are bringing. There could be several trucks or just a few trucks. So it is possible it can be one convoy or an accumulation of several convoys. In this case, I do not know. We made a [indiscernible] calculate, and so the number of kilos and litres which are here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Could that have been a reason to restrict the passage of convoys, the fact that they were abused by the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is far-fetched, as far as I'm concerned. Try to relate the two issues. The food supplies which were supposed to come in, what would happen the local people who had no other source of livelihood, and saying you can -- you know, you can restrict so that the food is not taken by the military, I think it's -- it's a bit selfish, in that the food distribution was being done in a proper manner and, secondly, there was a list kept by the UNHCR on who the recipients of these food items were and the next resupply. And always we used to request for authority for the UNHCR convoys to be allowed into the enclave in advance, because these people had no other source of resupply, so you cannot relate the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I am not looking for any justifications as to why the aid was provided to the army. Did the VRS ever complain about that, did they protest? Did they let you know that the BiH Army was abusing those convoys, especially fuel, and that is why there were restrictions on the supplies of fuel? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe a bit of correction before I answer that. Where you've said that you're not looking for any justification as to why the aid was provided to the army, I did not mention anything like that, that the aid was being provided to the army. Secondly, now coming to your question, there was no way that we knew that the Muslim Army was abusing the food convoys. On the contrary, the Bosnian Serb Army are the ones who are abusing these convoys, in that they were getting hold of the supplies before they enter Zvornik, and they get -- they remove whatever they want. Sometimes they could take whole convoys and they [indiscernible] them. Whole convoys and they [indiscernible] them, including even fuel, meant for the use by UNHCR and ICRC. So here we are looking at a very small quantity that is written here as compared to the amount that was taken by the Bosnian Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever see, or did you ever hear, or did the humanitarian aid -- the so-called UNHCR ever report to you that the entire convoy had been seized?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Entire convoys, in the sense that we're talking about even the vehicles, no. What I'm talking about is the supplies therein would be taken by the Bosnian Serb Army. It used to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: While we're on this page, Mr. President, I just note there are two indiscernibles on the transcript at lines 15 and 17, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I couldn't hear what the words were. I think it was the same word said twice, and it's not on the transcript. So if we could just have that clarification now, I think that would help the record, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You can look at the transcript. Now, nearly on the top, do you see that on lines 15 and 16? What were you saying? Do you remember? "Sometimes they could take whole convoys, and they ... them." What was the word you used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think what I meant was they could take the whole convoys, in terms of the amount inside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just what was the word you used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It sounded like "vet" or something like that, but I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is gone now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. At this point, I would like to give Judge Mindua the opportunity to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, since we are on this very important document, dated the 5th of June, 1995: Yesterday, you specified that you were unarmed and that you lived among the people. The UNMOs, I'm talking about the UNMOs. This document states that a large quantity of food had been withdrawn or separated for the benefit of the ABiH Army. I would like to ask you two short questions. Who was in charge of the distribution of the humanitarian aid that came from the UNHCR? And I shall now put my second question so that I don't need to take the floor again. Was it at all possible, at the time of the food distribution, to make a distinction between the Muslim civilians and the Muslim military, according to what you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the people who were to distribute the food were the UNHCR, themselves. They're the ones who are -- who had the total authority of distributing the food. They're the ones who kept the list of the recipients of the food items. On the issue of whether it was easy to distinguish between soldiers and non-soldiers during distribution is not a very easy thing to do. Definitely, they were not -- you know, when everybody lined up for food, it's those who need the food, as per the list that was being kept by UNHCR, so those are the ones who were entitled to get the food items. So it is very difficult to distinguish whether this one is a soldier. Provided they are not armed, they are not in uniform, they are just the normal people living in the village, they'll be given food. If one happens later on to have been a soldier, that is a different thing, but it was very difficult, actually, I can understand, for the UNHCR to distinguish who is a soldier and who is not when giving the supplies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. As an UNMO, when you were in Srebrenica, or in Tuzla, more specifically, you were unable to mark a distinction between the civilians and the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For sure, I was not in Tuzla. I was in Srebrenica. Secondly, I said we are not the ones who were giving out the food. It was the UNHCR, not UNMOs. Ourselves, we just go there to witness that the food distribution is taking place and that people are being given the right quantities of food items, and report on the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've understood that perfectly well. I've understood that it was not the UNMOs who distributed the food. But it was to move on to the question put by the Defence, because the Defence said that food supplies were carried out for the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I wanted to know from you, as an UNMO in the field, whether you were able to distinguish between these aid beneficiaries, whether you were able to make the difference between those people who were part of the military and those people who were civilians. I didn't say that you were actually distributing the food.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I get your point, sir. The issue at hand is distribution of food to the Bosnian Serb Army. That, for sure, never happened. As far as I know, it did not happen. There was no distribution of food to the Bosnian Serb Army. What I said thereafter is that when people are lining up to get the food supplies, sometimes you can have somebody who could be a soldier and get the normal food package. That does not mean that you are giving food supplies to the Bosnian Serb Army, because this is an independent person coming for his entitlement of food supplies, because the locals actually needed that food supply. But for -- the supply to the Bosnian Serb Army, as far as I know, never happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I clarify two matters. Are you really referring to the Bosnian Serb Army or to the Bosnian Muslim Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I meant the Muslim Army. There were no supplies being given to the Muslims' army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think everybody realised what you are referring to, but you said "Bosnian Serb Army." That was a mistake. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's the first point. The other is: While you were answering, we had a short discussion among the Judges. On page 12, lines 2 and 3, there is a sentence in the question of Judge Mindua: "This document states that a large quantity of food had been withdrawn or separated for the benefit of the ABiH Army." Reading this document on the screen carefully, we don't see a clear reference to this statement "for the benefit of the ABiH Army," but I just wanted to clarify that for the record and not to continue with this discussion. I think your position is quite clear. Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Presiding Judge was undoubtedly right to say something. But on looking at this document, dated the 5th of June, 1995, I can see -- I can read "Subject: Record of donation to the ABiH Army." That indicated that the food supplied were made for -- were intended for the ABiH Army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, Mr. President, there is no contest from the Prosecution that portions of the humanitarian aid made it to ABiH fighters who were in the Srebrenica enclave, and again that's Adjudicated Fact 47. That's not a contest. We don't view that as anything particularly, you know, like a big deal. Again, just so you know, that's not an issue, as far as the Prosecution is concerned. So we obviously recognise this refers to the BiH Army, and we understand that some of this food made it to fighters in the 28th Division in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I think now we should give Mr. Tolimir the opportunity to continue with his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This says clearly, in line number 2 -- sorry, first line, it says: "We hereby submit a list of the quantities of food, materiel and technical equipment and fuel issued to our military units ..." So not individuals, but military units for the month of May. It's a whole month. And please take into account another statement that says: "We wish to note that the above quantities were separated out of the humanitarian aid consignment which arrived in the area through UNHCR, while some of the food was obtained from the Dutch Battalion." This aid was not given to individuals waiting in a line. They were issued to a military unit. But I can't spend any more time on this. I have to move on to a different question. I suggest that this document be admitted into evidence, D70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was D80. I was told it was only marked for identification because a previous witness couldn't identify anything of the content of this document. Are you tendering it now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Taking into account what the witness was able to testify about, he couldn't say anything about the document, he has seen it today for the first time, he didn't remember Mr. Hasanovic, and, therefore, it will stay as marked for identification and not admitted into evidence. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Please, Witness, let us now look in e-court at your statement. It's P992, page 4, paragraph 2, line 4. It's about one-and-the-same problem. In English, it's page 5. We have this page now. We see the paragraph 2 and line 4: "He often demanded to convey to the BiH the message that the VRS is proposing to the Muslims to leave the enclave safely, with the escort of the VRS." Then on the same page, and that's the next page in English: "On another occasion when Vukovic was present, there was air activity heard in the area, and he told us to inform the UN not to attempt to antagonise them. He told us to report to the Muslims that they had to pack up and go, and if not, he would kill them all." You say that Vukotic and Nikolic more than once told you such things. Do you remember that? Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did. I remember very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you ever convey these things to the Muslims, what they said?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever put that forward at an official meeting, when all the three parties were present, the two opposing parties and the UNMOs and the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which opposing parties? I don't get the make-up. You are saying which opposing parties in the present -- when they are present?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I mean the Muslims and the Serbs. If they ever had a meeting together in your presence during your tenure, was that conveyed to the Muslims, what the Serbs said, and did the Muslims give any answer? Was this ever conveyed, these messages traded between the parties?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my tenure there, we never had a meeting of both sides present at one meeting. I don't remember at any time having met both sides together. But at least we could convey what we are told from one side to the other, because most of this information was meant to be conveyed through us to the other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, did this threat by Vukovic ever materialise, the one you state in paragraph 5? It's actually Nikolic's threat to the Muslims, that they had to pack up and go, and if not, he would kill them all. We should look now in e-court at 65 ter 1407, page 37 in Serbian and page 52 in English. That's the meeting in Fontana. Let us hear what the authorised person, the person with most authority on behalf of the VRS, says, and that's General Mladic. And my question is: Were these unofficial exchanges with Vukovic and Nikolic, who falsely represented themselves as commanders, ever comparable with the authorised view of the VRS? Were they ever understood as the official position of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is P1008, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can answer your question. For one -- for one, these are -- Major Nikolic and Colonel Vukovic were, as far as we knew, representatives of the Bosnian Serb Army. And even in meetings, like they could come in full army combat armed and with other senior officers, so we had no question -- we could not question whether they were part of the army. We knew they were. Secondly, these threats of wiping out the Muslims from the enclave actually happened. They ensured it happened, and that was through the whole process of bombarding the enclave from somewhere on the 6th. After that time, they cleared the whole enclave of the Muslims. So it was not just a threat. They ensured they achieved their objective. Initially, we were taking it as just a threat, and we conveyed the same to the Muslim side. We conveyed the same to our headquarters. But later on, it turned out, actually, it was a plan, it had already been pre-planned, and they ensured that they wiped or they removed the Muslims out of Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We'll now see the words of the person who was responsible, in the eyes of the law and in the eyes of the Court, to represent the Army of Republika Srpska. We have even seen the film where this can be seen, and now we can see the transcript. General Mladic says -- look at the last paragraph in Serbian, and in English that's the paragraph indicated as General Mladic speaking at the top: "You are in a position to know ..." I'm quoting General Mladic, and it's also on the film: "You are in a position to know ... You can, if everything is ready ... The rest of your army can disarm and surrender their weapons to UN officers -- to my officers," that is, "in the presence of UNPROFOR officers. You can choose to stay or you can choose to leave. If you wish to leave, you can go anywhere you like. When the weapons have been surrendered, every individual will go," will go, he guarantees this, "where they want to go. The only thing is that petrol must be provided, and I'll provide the vehicles. You can't provide the petrol. You can pay for it if you have the means." This meeting was the third meeting in Fontana between Mladic, Karremans, and the representatives of the Muslims. Did you know that this third meeting took place in Fontana, have you ever seen that film, and do you remember the words of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For one, I don't remember attending that meeting. Secondly, I think I've seen this film. And, thirdly, this is not the first time that General Ratko Mladic was saying that he'll provide a safe passage for these people to get out. To me, I think it was the second time, because he had earlier on told me that he has no problem with the people if they can move out of that enclave. That had also been conveyed earlier to us by Colonel Vukovic, who told us that he would like the Muslims -- the Bosnian Serb's army would like all the Muslims to leave the enclave, and if they agree to do that, they'll be given a safe passage out of the enclave, and that if they don't do that, he will wipe them all out. So that was the first time that we were told that. The second time is what I mentioned, when General Ratko Mladic told me that he will allow the people to get out of the enclave, and now I think this is -- at that time, he's saying that. But, of course, you are giving people safe passage after you've already bombarded the whole place, after you've already killed many of them, after you've harassed them with a lot of fire-power, artillery, tanks, and all that. That is the time you are trying to prove like you're being a bit humanitarian. I don't think that is the point. I don't think that shows a humanitarian face. You kill people, you bombard them throughout, harassing fire, and then after you have displaced all of them, that's the time, you know, you try to be a better humanitarian and tell them you can give them a safe passage out? I don't see any humanitarian face in the whole of that, that act.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please give me shorter answers. Did Mladic give this statement -- make this statement before the Muslims left or did he say that in his talks with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of your questions require a bit of clarification, because like that one, you know General Ratko Mladic did not arrive in the enclave before the onslaught. He arrived, actually, almost after; that is, after the place had been softened and all the people had come to the DutchBat compound. That is when he came in. So already all these bombardments had already been done, and that is the time he was talking like this. This was much, much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that issue of how people arrived at the base and who brought them. But let us now show in e-court P992. That's the statement of this witness, page 9 in Serbian, paragraph 5, where the witness describes his meeting with General Mladic on the 12th of July, 1995. We can see it now. In English, it's page 11. I will quote what you said: "The soldiers of the VRS patrolled among the refugees along the road --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be better for everybody if you indicate which paragraph you are quoting. You are always indicating the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, it's page 11, third paragraph. And in Serbian, it's the fifth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would save time if you, just from the beginning, could indicate the right document number, the right page number, and the right paragraph number. We are now waiting for page 11. Is that page 11? I see "9." Okay, it might be page 11. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is page 11 in e-court. The statement in English contains two pages which are not contained in the Serbian version of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm quoting what you said in your statement: "VRS soldiers patrolled the refugees around the road. Around noon, I heard rumours about Mladic being there. I saw a group of VRS soldiers as well as UNPROFOR troops. I recognised Mladic among them talking with refugees. I approached him, and he started to talk with me informally about Kenya, because it was written on a patch of my uniform that I was from Kenya. I then informed him that the UN proposed to assist in the evacuation of the refugees by providing transportation. He answered that he didn't need the UN because he had enough vehicles for those people and that the buses were on their way already. He said that all the refugees would be transported to Tuzla. Then we stopped the conversation, and I continued to take care of the refugees." Sir, did I read out correctly what you stated about what the conversation between you and Mladic was about? Was your statement correct or is what you're saying here correct? Are you interpreting something or misinterpreting, or what happened? Why the discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If there is some alleged discrepancy, if General Tolimir could indicate what this alleged discrepancy is, between what and what. He's just read him a part of the statement, but he's not referring the witness to anything when he suggests that there's some discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's take things at a time with brief questions and brief answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please don't interrupt me. If I give you the floor, then you may proceed. I think this witness is capable and able to answer the question. I was astonished by your -- by the way you put the question to the witness, but I think he will manage to answer. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did this happen on the 12th? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it was on the 12th. I'm not very sure of the date, but I think it's the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And before that, did a meeting take place between Karremans and General Mladic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think there was a meeting that had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you learn anything about that meeting, and is that why you offered transportation and help with the evacuation, or did you receive an instruction from your superiors?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were doing our work as military observers, people employed by the United Nations, and we had to get further people who were already displaced. We had requested -- we were informing our headquarters of everything that was going on, and we used to request whatever we need for the people of the enclave. In this particular circumstance, we knew, actually, the people had to be evacuated from Srebrenica to a safer place, so we had requested for transport. And the UN had agreed that they were going to send buses to transport the people from the enclave so that they can get out of that misery. And so I was just telling General Ratko Mladic how it was; that the UN is prepared to get the Muslims out of the enclave because it was no longer tenable, it was no longer safe for them to continue staying there. They were no longer living in their houses. They had been displaced. It was a humanitarian catastrophe, and the UN could not just watch that continue, since the Bosnian Serbs' army were already all over the enclave. They had even started occupying -- and it is in my statement. They had already started occupying some of the houses. They had already started -- you know, I don't know the right word, but taking away - I want to say stealing - but taking away even cows, going as far as even removing the cows, the beddings, the mattresses all that, from those houses, taking them all the way towards Bratunac. In fact, that is they were vandalising everywhere, they were taking everything. So it was no longer, as far as we observers were concerned, tenable for the Muslims to continue staying there. And the last part of it I can say was that this was just a confirmation of the initial threats that we had received of removing every Muslim person from the enclave, from Colonel Vukovic and also from Major Nikolic, so we knew they were just acting -- they were just doing what they had planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We have your statement. We know what you stated. Just tell us now: Did VRS troops, before the evacuation, carry mattresses and blankets and enter the houses, or were they outside of any Muslim settlements, without any contacts with the Muslim population there? Thank you. You have just told us that you saw them patrolling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For sure, this was happening, it was ongoing; that is, the taking away of household items, taking away of cows and goods. We could see them, you know, moving along the main road heading towards Bratunac. That was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well, very well. But was that before this event or after this event? Thank you. Thank you. Please, tell us, and I apologise to the interpreters and everybody else, was this before your conversation with Mladic or after? This is all I'm interested in. Before or after, before or after, just say "before" or "after," that's it.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was during and after.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to observe that or did you hear about that? If that taken place before, could you have warned Mladic about that? You stated that you only saw the soldiers patrolling and that you heard about Mladic coming. That's all you stated.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at some of our sitrep situation reports, that is indicated, that that was happening, and it continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, it doesn't really matter that much. We don't want to dwell upon that any longer. And now, let's see, who was it who insisted on what you heard -- told Mladic? Where you authorised to tell him that? Did you receive an instructions to that effect from your superiors? You offered him to evacuate the people. Who instructed you to offer that to Mladic on the 12th? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said much earlier that we were in direct communication with our headquarters, and we told them what was going on. We advised them that there is need to evacuate the Muslims, and they advised that they are going to send the buses to evacuate the Muslims from the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you agree to that with your superiors? When did you learn that? When did you receive that, what you later on conveyed to Mladic, that information? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was before I informed General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now could the Court please produce 65 ter 1407. That's from the first meeting at Fontana Hotel. In order not to waste time with watching the video, because there is a video and the sound recording, I'm just displaying the transcript of what had transpired at that meeting. Page 16 in Serbian; 19 in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it would be helpful and save time to indicate and -- to ask the witness to read that for his own, and not to quote the whole part of that, because we have, I suppose, much of them already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It is very important for me to quote the first sentence here. In his statement, the witness said that he did not remember who was it who asked for the meeting, whether it was Karremans or Mladic. That's what the witness said in his statement. Later on, we'll see where that is. That's why I have to read to him who it was who asked for the meeting to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General Mladic, the last paragraph on the right-hand side in the Serbian language, and it says, and I quote: "What do you want?" He says: "What do you want? You asked for a meeting. Speak up." That's what General Mladic said. And then -- he said that to Colonel Karremans, of course. And then Colonel Karremans replied to General Mladic: "I had a talk with General Nicolai two hours ago ..." And I'm reading just this sentence here: "... and also with the national authorities about the request on behalf of the population." And then perhaps the witness can go on reading the text for himself, and then I'll have a question for him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, your question, please. The witness is waiting for your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: In your statement, you said that you didn't know who asked for the meeting to take place between Karremans and Mladic. And now, based on this, what you have before you, can you tell us who requested for the meeting to take place? Was it Karremans or was it Mladic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm seeing this write-up. But from the write-up, you can see it's Karremans -- Colonel Karremans who requested further meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It's clear from the contents, is it not? And now there is no need for me to display a statement. It's on page 8 in the Serbian version, paragraph 6, where you say, and I am going to quote, and if you don't agree, you tell me: "I wanted to have a meeting with the VRS in the evening. That's why I contacted Peter. I don't know who asked for that meeting. Was it the VRS of Colonel Karremans?" Do you remember that, and did I quote your statement correctly, the two lines that I've just read? Page 8, paragraph 6, lines 1 and 2, for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we have said -- as I have said, I said that this meeting was called by Colonel Karremans, and he had the right to call a meeting. Me, I was not sure whether it's him who had called for the meeting, when I was writing this statement, or not. But now we can see it's him who had requested for the meeting. Secondly, the issue you have brought out, that of the request for the buses, we, as military observers, and I need to repeat that, requested through the normal channels. It was not in reference to this meeting. It was through our own channels that we did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you look carefully at your words, and I will quote your words again: "I contacted Peter to organise the meeting in the evening with the BSA." That you means that you also participated in the organisation of this meeting; yes or no? That's an inference I'm making from this sentence.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I request you bring that one here so that I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is P992 again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. Can the Court please display, firstly, the witness's statement, which is P992, page 8 in Serbian and page 10 in English. The first sentence in the sixth paragraph. Thank you. We still don't see the English version of the document. And now we can see the fourth paragraph from the bottom, the first sentence: "I contacted Petar to organise a meeting in the evening with the VRS."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you state that? Did you organise the meeting that Karremans called for, the meeting with Mladic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the most important thing is to interpret the whole thing as it is. For the UNPROFOR to have meetings, most of that time they had to go through us to organise the meeting through Peter, so what I meant here is that I could not remember whether it is the BSA side who had requested for this meeting or Colonel Karremans. Colonel Karremans could not -- you know, could not be able to organise the meeting unless, you know, they went through us to organise with Peter, because he had our communication. And so the issue on whether I can remember who did this or that, it's true, I could not remember who it was, Colonel Karremans or BSA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're on this topic - I love a good mystery as much as the next person - I'm just wondering if General Tolimir can tell us what the relevance of this line of questioning is. I'm mean, I'm happy to hear it, but I'm just wondering, like, who cares who called the meeting, and why is it important? Maybe that would help in some way. But if we could just have some idea of why we're spending so much time on the topic of who called for the meeting, it might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am emphasising the contradiction in the statement. In the first statement, he says that he called Peter to arrange the meeting, and then in the third sentence he says that he doesn't know who called the meeting. This is a contradiction. I want to clarify things, just as the witness, himself, said here, that things need to be clarified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you may make your conclusions as you want, but to put it to the witness in that way, I think it's not correct. The witness has answered and explained from his point of view. You may have another point of view, but I think it is quite clear what the witness was able to provide, and you should leave that point and continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's very important because of the things that he was saying. He said that he spoke to General Mladic on the 12th, and he told us what General Mladic had told him. And before that, he was the one who called the meeting on the 12th. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it is not helpful to have this kind of discussion between the parties and the Chamber. You are cross-examining the witness, and you should do that. Please carry on, and don't explain always why you are putting a question. Please just carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We heard from your answers that VRS soldiers contacted the civilians and to the village even before the evacuation. Could you please tell us this: Did VRS soldiers contact with the refugees in the base in Potocari while men were being separated from the women, while women went their way, and the men, on the other hand, started preparing their breakthrough on the other side? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you can start by explaining what this separation was all about. We had two groups. In fact, I can call them three groups of IDPs. One was inside the Dutch compound, inside the warehouse. There was a smaller group outside the compound, but still within DutchBat. And that and the biggest group was in the warehouse just before you get to the DutchBat compound on your way from Srebrenica. Going down, it was on the right-hand side. So these were the three groups. But the biggest, as I said, was that one, you know, outside. The BSA soldiers, after the, you know, the enclave was overwhelmed and everybody had been brought to Potocari, they started patrolling the streets, going up -- all the way up to Srebrenica and occupying those areas. This was -- that was the final assault, actually, by the infantry; that is, the mopping up to ensure that there are no soldiers. So after that, the separation of the men from the women and children started. This was being done by the BSA soldiers. They removed the men from the women and children and sent them to a house, a white house. And because this is all listed here, I don't know whether you still want me to continue with the same thing, because it's all written. They were separated from the women and kept in one house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I have that. I'm going to ask you something about that so-called white house, but I'm asking you this before that: Muslim women and men, when they left their houses, were they separated? Did women and children go one way and did men go another way? Just tell me that, if you know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the we saw is women -- in fact, family units going together with their belongings to Potocari. Those who managed to go inside the DutchBat went there. Those who could not sat outside there as family units, even when they were out there, they were sort of organised in family units, together with the men, those family units which were headed by men, or just women and children. So they were there as units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that Muslim civilians were not separated, women and children were not separated from men, that they all arrived in Potocari? We had witnesses here who testified that they had been separated from their families, that they had been brought to a different place - thank you - and that from that place they started to organise a breakthrough. Do you know anything about that breakthrough? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, you can't rule that out. It's not possible for all of them to have gone there as single units, complete units. Maybe some of them joined them later. That is possible. In any war -- in any war scenario, that is possible. But the way we saw them outside there before the separation by the Bosnian Serb Army, they were together, all of them, you know, together, both men, women, and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we then conclude that the VRS carried out the separation, and that before that, women were not separated from men in Srebrenica? Yes or no? What can the Trial Chamber conclude? What kind of conclusions can they make? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusion that can be made out of that is that the BSA soldiers separated the men from the women and children and took them to one definite house. The separation that could have been there earlier --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you give me one second. The separation that could have been there before they arrived at Potocari, that was because it's unavoidable. During war, some people can run faster than others. But later on, they regrouped and became one, until they were separated by the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did Becirovic go? Did he also arrive in Potocari? Thank you. Since you said that all of them found themselves together eventually? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, I would be unable to understand where we are heading to here, because if you're going to talk about each and every individual, I did not know these people, all of them. If you're going to ask whether so-and-so was there or whatever, I do not do that, I could not have been able to know all that. But the point is that we could see men, women, and children together. Do not expect me to know whether each man that I saw was the head of that family. It is difficult for me to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question to you is this: Did you hear that Becirovic also had provided a statement, just like you, that he said that he was not alone, that there were 11.000 people with him who had left Srebrenica? Thank you. Are you aware of that? Did you hear of that at all - thank you - at previous trials or during your stay in Srebrenica - thank you - did you know that men, soldiers went a separate way and that they had sent their women to Potocari? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say men left Srebrenica in a separate way, I'm unable to understand what you mean, because even in the video, in my statement, and in all documentation, there were men in Potocari, there were men who came there. It is evident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't need any more explanation. I just asked you whether everyone came to Potocari, men and women and children, men who did fight and men who didn't fight. Let's go back to that house. That's page 9 of your statement, paragraph 6 - that's in Serbian - lines 1 and 2, and in English it's two pages further. It's page 11 in English. This is the right page. I will quote from your statement: "I began to notice that BSA --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May we get the paragraph number of the English page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Serbian, it's 9; in English, it's 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm asking for the paragraph number in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My legal assistant will tell you in a moment, because I don't know English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the witness doesn't know B/C/S. That's the problem. And if you want to show him the relevant part of the statement, you should indicate which part he should read in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Third full paragraph in English on this page we are looking at. Thank you, Aleksandar. Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not going to ask my question before the witness has had a chance to read it, and I will read it myself. I quote: "I began to notice that BSA soldiers were separating men from their families and were leading them towards a white house located just in front of the compound, slightly on the left ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On the same page, you go on to say that you went to that house with Mladic, followed by a camera. It's paragraph 7. You say he was accompanied by a TV crew. My question is: Did I read this out correctly? Were you, indeed, in that white house with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did a TV crew follow you into that house?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Inside the white house, did you see any children, little children? Because you say that even boys were separated. That's in your statement. Were any boys inside the white house, and did the camera record that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are taking it out of context. These are two different sections of my statement. The one you quoted earlier, that is, concerning General Ratko Mladic in the house, and that of when I noticed some boys being taken to the white house or being removed from the buses, those are two different scenarios, and I'll start with the first one. When I went to talk to General Ratko Mladic outside there -- now, when I went to talk to him and discuss about the white house, he said that, actually, those people have got no problems. And he agreed, after a request, to escort me there to see that there were no problems with those people in the white house. That is when the TV crew followed us, but that was after some time. It delayed a bit. At that time, I could notice they were taking some supplies, that of soft drinks and some beer, to the white house. And then upon arrival, when we arrived there, they already were distributing, and the crew was filming, and General Ratko Mladic was telling me, Can't you see they are okay? They are feeling good? And it was true, when you look at them at that particular time when they were receiving those supplies, they look happy, but it was because they were very hungry, very thirsty, exhausted, and uncertain of their future. So whatever little they are given, they appreciate, and, you know, they look like they are okay. And I've already mentioned it here, but according to me, this was like acting in a film. You know, it's like you want to portray you're doing something good to the people. Yet, these are the same people you have harassed. So the second one, the separation you are talking about -- I hasten to add that inside the house or within that house, I did not see boys, and I've not mentioned it anywhere. After that, during when the men -- the families, that is, the children and the women, and the older group of men, were being loaded into the buses, that is when the BSA soldiers started even picking some boys who were as young as about 14 years, and I even asked one of them how old he was, and he said, Fourteen years. From that time, I started, you know, telling them to go back. I started, you know, trying to communicate with the BSA soldiers, and they refused to let the boys go back. But when I hold one of the boys and tell him to go back to the bus, somehow the soldiers allowed that to happen. They went back to the buses, most of them went back, managed to go back. But as I turned to another direction, I could see some of those boys I had told to go back being still taken back to the white house. So for sure I do not know how many of those boys were taken back, but I know some were removed from the buses. And my intervention helped some, but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think we are running out of time. The tapes have to be rewound and we need a technical break. We will have our first break of today, and we will resume a little bit earlier than usual. That means, in this case, 12.30, half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You spoke on several occasions about separation and about some warehouse premises where Nikolic ran checks; that you went inside there and that you looked at him while he was checking on some lists, whether those separated people had participated in certain actions where war crimes had been committed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember talking about Major Nikolic going into DutchBat compound, into the warehouse where some of the IDPs were, and was checking the men against a list that he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's correct. Did you have access there? Did anyone enable you to see the men he was checking against that list?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was there. I was there, physically. I could see him going to the men. Then he could call one man, then ask his name, you go through the list that he had and check whether -- I think the main aim was to check whether they were soldiers or not, because that list, I think, contained a list of those they knew as soldiers from the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's page 11 on your statement, paragraph 1. Line 9 in Serbian, and that's page 11 in English. I'll give you the number of the paragraph when it shows up on the screen. Can we have in e-court your statement P992. We see it on the screen now. Let's just have page 11 in Serbian and page 13 in English. Here, you say in line 1: "Since the VRS asked to check inside the base to see whether there were any armed soldiers inside ..." And then in line 5 -- in English, it would be paragraph 2, I think -- no, in English it's the first one we see, where it says how Nikolic was running checks inside the compound, and in line 9 in Serbian you say: "The name of every person checked was sought in the list that Nikolic had." Just tell me, did Nikolic separate any of those people who were under the control of the UNPROFOR after checking their names against that list?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember very well, I think there was only one person that he took who was injured. I think -- I think there's only one person that he took, nobody else, if I can remember very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he take that person away because they were injured or because that person was for some reason suspect, and what happened later to that person?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was taken due to both reasons. That is, he was injured. Secondly, he was suspected by Major Nikolic, you know, according to the list that he had, to be a soldier on the Muslim side, so he took him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what happened to that man or do you know his name so we can check whether he is among the missing persons, because everyone was registered as missing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 2 on page 11 in the Serbian version, you say: "Major Nikolic also requested we provide him with the list of the local staff who would be evacuated together with the DutchBat. "The list was prepared by MSF ..." My question is: First of all, have you found it in the English text?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Correct, that's paragraph 2. Did Major Nikolic separate anyone from that list of local staff that you gave him, the local staff that was supposed to be evacuated together with the Dutch?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We gave him the list that was prepared by MSF and us and is available somewhere here. That was included all the local people who were working with the NGOs. And the list, I think we went through it yesterday or the day before. So the -- he did not -- there's nobody who was removed, as far as I can remember, from amongst those who were in that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Do you know that the OTP has a list of missing persons who were reported as gone missing during the separation and from the column that went with Becirovic, trying to break out towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of such a list. I've heard of it. I've never seen it, but I've heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that this list contains indications of who went missing, where, and who went missing in Potocari, because the families reported when they last saw them? And do you have any knowledge whether there are children under 15 on that list, because you said a moment ago there were boys of 14?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that list. I have not seen it, that's what I said, so I do not know what is contained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that we have heard witnesses here whose children had gone missing, and that they testified about the way their children went missing, and they said nobody detained children, but they released them instead? And do you know that one such child at the time testified in this case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Honestly, Mr. President, we need some basis for this, what witness are we allegedly talking about, so we can have some sense of where this comes from. I mean, this is such a general question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the Chamber would appreciate more details as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I cannot give names because these are protected witnesses who testified here. There was even one witness, if you remember, whom I didn't want to question. I'm not giving the witness names and details, to ask him about the identity of the person. I'm just asking him this in order to ask later whether he had seen someone killed on the 12th or the 13th, the time he describes as the time of separation of refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know if General Tolimir is changing his question, but the prior question had, as one of its components, referring to some witness or witnesses, "they said nobody detained children, but they released them instead." We're simply asking General Tolimir what the basis is for that statement in his question. And then he referred, as another component of the question: "Do you know that one such child at the time testified in this case?" So if he has evidence that there was somebody who testified about a missing relative or something like that, and then there was that relative actually testifying, allegedly, according to General Tolimir, we'd like to know who he's talking about. If he's moving on, Mr. President, then I'll sit down and stay down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed -- [Overlapping speakers] Mr. Tolimir, wait, please. If you are referring to a witness we have heard in closed session, then you can't put a question to this witness, if he knows that there was a witness testifying in closed session. This makes no sense, so that perhaps you'll rephrase your question or carry on with another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I thank Mr. Thayer. I have no time for this. I will move to another topic. And I cannot name them because they were protected witnesses, except by the numbers, but these were witnesses who testified in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You spoke in your statement, on page 8, paragraph 2 in Serbian, line 5, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please give us the English version, including the paragraph, for the sake of the witness and the interpreters and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Serbian, it's page 8, paragraph 2, line 5 and 6. And in English, it's page 10. When we see the text on the screen, I will tell you which line it is. Line -- sorry, paragraph 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see paragraph 4, where you say, in lines 5 and 6: "At that time, a river of refugees arrived at the compound in Potocari. Very soon, the base was full, and people had to remain outside." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see the paragraph that begins with: "In the afternoon, I was in Potocari. Emir had returned the previous evening. We had no communication about the situation in Srebrenica. The information in the sitrep originates from the DutchBat"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be helpful to give a correct reference. We found now a paragraph on I think it's page 8: "During the morning, I was in Potocari." Are you referring to that passage? In that case, you should quote correctly and not say "in the afternoon" instead of "in the morning," or there is a problem of translation. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The original in Serbian says: "During the morning, I was in Potocari." I'm sorry, I don't speak English. I'm not paraphrasing; I'm quoting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us on which day that was? Was it in the morning or the afternoon? What does it say in English, because I can't understand it? Can you tell us the exact date and time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the morning. For the day, I can't remember whether it was the 11th or 12th. I'm not very sure. But it was in the morning, as indicated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It must have been on the 11th, and that's why I asked you, because in the previous paragraph you say that the DutchBat received another ultimatum on the 10th of July, and the UN sent an ultimatum to the Army of Republika Srpska that by 0600 hours they must withdraw from the base; otherwise, there would be air-strikes. That's page 8 in Serbian and page 7 in English. It's on the screen. It's the paragraph where the first sentence refers to the DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, on the basis of the fact that this happened on the 10th, can you determine that the next paragraph refers to the 11th? And when was it that the refugees arrived at the base, on the 10th or the 11th? Shall I rephrase the question? Can you tell me when the refugees came for the first time to the base in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not very sure, but I think it was on the 11th, either 10th or 11th. I'm not very sure of that, but it's indicated somewhere in my -- in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the Muslim population arriving at the base before the meetings between Mladic and Karremans on the 11th, and before you called Peter to organise the meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me to explain a bit on this. This meeting that Colonel Karremans talked about at the ultimatums, it was held at night, and that is the time we were told about those ultimatums and what they mean, because the ultimatums were from both sides, the BSA and also from the UN. And the Muslims actually heard about them, and they gave their concerns as indicated. As for the meeting with General Mladic and Colonel Karremans, that was held, I think -- I think later, because by the time we were holding that meeting with -- that meeting was being held with General Mladic, the IDPs were already -- had already gone to Potocari. They were already in Potocari at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In order for us to be able to follow the chronology of your statement, tell me, first, what you know about the meeting with Karremans where those ultimatums were presented by the Muslims and the Serbs and the UNPROFOR. That was on the 11th. What do you know about that, so we can follow the events chronologically?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, these ultimatums, if I can explain, the one from the BSA side, they had said that the Muslims and UNPROFOR should lay down their weapons, and then the Muslims would be allowed a safe passage out. There would be no more bombardment of the enclave. Then the UN ultimatum was for the Muslims -- for the Bosnian Serb Army to stop shelling the enclave. Otherwise, there would be air-strikes on their positions. I think those were the main -- the major ultimatums that were there. I think there was another one on who was to go to DutchBat compound. The BSA had said that only the UN people, that is, UNMOs, UNPROFOR, UNHCR and, I think, Red Cross, would go there, but no Muslims should be allowed to go there. That was -- those were the ultimatums that were given. But in this meeting, this is not the meeting that General Ratko Mladic was in. This is a different meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that it was not that meeting. First of all, there was a Karremans meeting with the Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are not giving evidence. The witness is giving evidence. What you knew, it's not important at this point in time. You should put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Let's begin like this: Page 7 of the witness's statement, paragraph 10, the last three lines in Serbian, that's where it begins with the words "Colonel Karremans," and in English it's page 9. Page 7 in Serbian, and page 9 in English. It's the right page on the screen. I quote: "Colonel Karremans informed those present that he had received an ultimatum the previous day from the Army of Republika Srpska and explained its terms to the local officials, telling them that he had rejected it. I learned about this ultimatum just before the meeting -- just before the meeting. He then explained ..." And then let's move to the next page, page 8 in Serbian -- 8, not 9: "He then explained that --" It's page 8 we need, not 9: "He then explained that the Dutch battalion received another ultimatum on the 10th of July, which was also rejected, and that in its turn the UN sent an ultimatum to the VRS to withdraw from the enclave by 0600 hours. If they do not, there would be air-strikes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just so the witness can follow along, we need to be on page 9 of the English, which is page 7 of the document, itself. So if we're looking at the lower right-hand page number, we need to go just one more in the English to page 7, and we're talking about the large paragraph a couple of paragraphs up from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think page 9 of the document should be page 11 --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Page 7 of the statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is page 9 in e-court, yes. It's always going to be two pages off because there were two pages of another matter, a related matter, at the front of this statement. So there we are. We're talking about the paragraph that begins: "In the night, there was a problem ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see that now, thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your assistance, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
