utterances.text: Witness, did you hear what I have just read in your own language, in English, and were you able to read in your statement what you previously stated, and did you understand it so as to be able to answer when I put my question to you; yes or no? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you attend that meeting when Colonel Karremans was speaking about the various ultimatums? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did it say then, clear and loud, that one of the ultimatums was not to allow the Muslim population to enter the base in Potocari; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness was waiting until you are able to listen to his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Your Honour, that was one of the conditions given at that time from the BSA side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does that mean that, in addition to that condition that Karremans rejected, or despite that condition, as a matter of fact, the Muslim population was able to enter the DutchBat base in Potocari; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true, and I said that earlier, that the Muslims had nowhere else to go. They had to go to a safer place, and the only safe place at that particular moment in time was in DutchBat compound. Do not forget that that is also where we went to because we were no longer safe in Srebrenica town.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now could the Court please produce D70 -- no, no, no, not D70. I apologise. 1D72, page 3. The document number is 1D72. Paragraphs 2, 3 and 4, please. The same page in English. And I'm reading for the transcript just one part of paragraph 2, where it says: "On the 10th of July -- on the 10th of July, around 1600 hours --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last paragraph in English, the last paragraph on page 2 that we see in front of us. And I'm reading from page 3, for the record, page 3, paragraph 2, in Serbian. And in English, it's page 2, in the last paragraph, where it says: "At about 1600 hours on 10 July 1995, Sergeant-Major van Schaik ordered us to leave the shelter. We were told to form a line together with the infantry in order to lead the refugees who were starting to arrive in the base. I will draw a green dotted line to demonstrate the line where we were standing. When I say 'refugees,' I mean Muslim refugees." Can we have the following page in English. Thank you. And now we are moving on to the fourth paragraph: "On the same day --" The third paragraph only has one sentence, and that's why I'm moving on to paragraph 4. And the third one says: "At that moment, the BSA was not in the compound in Potocari. "On the same day, four-ton UN trucks arrived from the direction of Bravo Company. The trucks were packed with refugees, men, women, elderly people and children. In one day, the compound filled up with refugees. I estimate the total at something like 2.000 people. Bravo Company is stationed at Srebrenica." Thank you, end of quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, for the record, it would be necessary to indicate this is a statement of a witness, Colonel Groenewegen, given to the OTP. I don't know the date. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 29th September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we get too bogged down in the witness statement of another witness who's already testified here, I would ask that General Tolimir provide for the Trial Chamber some idea of where he's going with this line of questioning. If it is to somehow impeach the witness's recollection of certain dates or events, that's fine. We've got no problem with that, obviously. But if General Tolimir is going to be challenging certain historically-established, fundamental, and, as I understand it, heretofore unchallenged elements of this case, for example, that the VRS entered Potocari for the first time in the morning of 12 July, that the buses arrived in the afternoon of 12 July, that the removal of the Muslim population began sometime in the afternoon of 12 July and continued to the 13th of July, if he is going to be challenging those fundamental elements of this case, we need to know that now, because -- and I don't want to say much more in front of the witness. But I think we need to hear from General Tolimir where he's going with this line of questioning, because I can get up and do a lot more stuff in redirect, as I know the Trial Chamber prefers, but at the same time I think we can possibly save a lot of time if we just understand what he intends to do with a witness statement of a witness who's already been here and testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I asked the witness whether he remembered if Muslim civilians had been in the base before General Mladic asked for nobody to enter the base. If you remember, the witness could not know exactly -- could not remember whether that was on the 10th or the 11th, before or after the meeting with Karremans. Now I quoted from a document to jog the witness's memory that that was on the 10th, and that in the morning the Muslims were still in the base in Potocari, or, rather, they had already arrived in the base in Potocari. Now I'm going to ask him whether they were or whether they were not. And I would kindly ask Mr. Thayer not to put 20 questions in his objection, because that has an impact on the further course of my cross-examination of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The problem is that you are using a document -- a statement of another witness. I don't know if that is the right way to jog the memory of the present witness, Mr. Kingori, here in the courtroom. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is precisely my point. If we look further into this witness statement, it is crystal clear that in his OTP witness statement, Mr. Groenewegen was off by one day about these fundamental events. He has chosen a witness statement in which there is an obvious error that I don't think anybody disputes here, and he's using that to cross-examine this witness to challenge his credibility. That is why I objected when I did, Mr. President, before this goes any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that we have to be very careful, if we put statements of other witnesses to a present witness, because we are not in the position to check if there is a mistake in this statement of the previous witness, Groenewegen, if he testified in the same way when he was here testifying in this trial. We can't do that, and this is not the proper way to challenge the credibility of the present witness. If you doubt what Mr. Kingori is telling you after your questions, then you should put documents related to him as a witness; perhaps his own statement, as you did before, or previous testimony in another trial. But it is not appropriate to put this statement another witness gave to the OTP to this witness to jog his memory, because we can't check, at this point in time, which one is correct, and it's not the duty of the Chamber to do that. We will give weight to all these documents and all the evidence at the end of the trial. I would like to ask Mr. Tolimir to remove this document from the screen and go ahead with his questioning with this witness, in order to save time. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, I want to make the Prosecution's general position clear from our perspective. We don't have a problem, as we have not had a problem during the trial, with General Tolimir using somebody else's statement. As we've seen, he's done that with testimony, he's done that with witness statements, and we have no problem with him doing that. That's fine with us. As I said, the problem here, as I see it, is that we are dealing with such central issues that simply cannot, under any reasonable interpretation, as I see it, be in dispute, and I'm inviting the Defence to let the Chamber know whether those issues are in dispute. I mean, if it is in dispute in this case that the VRS entered Potocari on another day, other than the morning of the 12th, or that the transportations began on the 12th continued on the 13th and were completed by the end of the 13th, then that really affects how we, to some degree, need to gauges how to present our evidence, if that's in context. And, again, that's part of the mischief I wanted to avoid with the use of -- the choice of this particular document, and I just wanted to make our position clear with respect to both of those matters, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At this point in time, our position was a little bit different, but that doesn't matter. We kindly ask Mr. Tolimir to proceed without this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We will introduce this document through other witnesses who were there together with this witness. But I had to jog the witness's memory, because he claims that he doesn't know when the refugees arrived in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the Chamber has ruled on that. Jog the memory of the witness with other documents, if you want. Continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question for the witness: Were the United Nations involved in transporting the refugees to Potocari in their vehicles before the 11th, before the Karremans-Mladic meeting took place? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no involvement of the UN transport in bringing people -- the IDPs to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can you please say what was it that Colonel Karremans said at the meeting that you attended, together with the Muslims? What did he say? What would transpire on the 11th, how the developments would evolve? We heard about the ultimatums. What ultimatum did he address at the army, and what were the contents of that particular ultimatum; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I've already said about the ultimatums.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, we have this answer on page 48, line 14, to 49, line 6. Sorry. 46, line 14, through 47, line 6.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I asked the witness everything else, not about the ultimatums. I wanted to know what Karremans said to the Muslims, because that was a meeting with the local Muslims. What else did he tell them about what would happen on the 11th? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Mr. Tolimir, this is now a new question. The previous one was exactly related to ultimatums. This is now a new question, and we would like to hear the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, when the Muslims were told about the ultimatums in this particular meeting, they were a bit apprehensive. They were not sure that the BSA side was sincere in what they were saying, that they would give a safe passage if they hand over all their weapons. And I remember -- I think it was Ramiz Becirovic asking Colonel Karremans whether he actually believed what the BSA have said. For sure, even for us, we could not believe, you know, what they had said. The other concern that the Muslims had was on the air-strikes. When Colonel Karremans told them that the UN had given the BSA an ultimatum of stopping to shell Srebrenica -- that they stop shelling Srebrenica, that they withdraw to the former positions beyond the cease-fire line, the Muslim -- and that if they don't do that by the next morning, at around 6.00 a.m., the fighters would be sent, that is, the aircraft to come and attack their positions. And I remember the Muslims doubting whether the UN would be able to do that. First of all, whether the BSA will withdraw; secondly, whether, if they refuse to withdraw, whether the UN will be able to carry out the air attacks. So these were some of the main concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was there an agreement reached between the United Nations and the Muslims about co-operation during the NATO aviation air-strikes? Did Karremans say anything to the Muslims about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you may explain a bit. Co-operation in what terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, for example, that Muslims should be allowed to pull out from the positions that the NATO would bomb, that a death zone would be created around Srebrenica. Did you hear any such thing? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember -- I cannot be able to recall any co-operation in the way that you are putting it. All I know is that we had given the grid references to the UN of the BSA positions that we already had. That included the artillery weapons, the tanks, and all that. So the UN headquarters already had those. But as to whether the Muslims would co-operate with the UN, I do not -- I do not recall that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Karremans try to convince the Muslims to try and pull out from a certain area because the NATO aviation would turn such zone into a death zone? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the witness please be shown 1D239, 19239. It's an excerpt from a show that was broadcast by the Radio Television of Serbia. Do we need to see the clip once again, Your Honours? The time is very restricted. Would it suffice for me to read the transcript of the show? Maybe the witness can read the transcript for himself, because the transcript is in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The transcript is on the screen now. Could you indicate which part of the English version the witness should read?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. He can read the entire transcript, and I would like the second paragraph to be entered into the record because I'm going to read it, with your leave, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should decide what you want to do. You asked the witness to read it. Then you should wait a moment and then put a question to the witness. The witness has read it. Put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does information conveyed by Meholjic and Nuhanovic in the passage you just read about the so-called death zone tally with your statement? Thank you. Does this reflect what you know and what you heard at the meeting? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it does not. There's nowhere that we were told about a death zone where two, four, a hundred feet, or whatever, would be bombarded. We were not aware of that. All I know is that we had clearly given the grid references of the BSA positions, the tanks and all that. Secondly, there was another British officer who was also giving --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you want an answer then you should listen to the answer. The witness stopped because you were in discussion with your legal adviser. Please continue your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. They also saw another officer from, I think, the British Army. We used to call them --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... who actually was also giving the same grid references, in as far as he could be able to get the BSA positions. So the UN headquarter, as such, or the NATO had those grid references. We do not require to declare one area a death zone, or death trap, or whatever, and there is nothing like that normally in such a condition, and especially where the UN attacks are concerned. The bombardment these days is not on how big an area you bombard. It is on how accurate you hit the target that you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber, what was your source of information about the upcoming bombardment of the VRS positions around Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope you're talking about the air-strikes, which we actually got from the UN headquarters. We are talking about through the chain all the way up to Zagreb. We got the information, and Colonel Karremans also had gotten the same, and that is exactly what he was conveying to both sides. He had conveyed the same to both sides, that is, to the Muslim side and to the BSA side, that if those conditions were not met, there would be air-strikes. And, in fact, we had requested for air-strikes much, much earlier, when the attacks started on the enclave, so we thought -- to us, we thought the UN had let us down, in that could they have come earlier and in full force, that we had requested, maybe the attack -- or the suffering of the people there could have been minimised, or the BSA could have been forced into a negotiating table so that we stop the war on Srebrenica. So it was -- it was a surprise that it delayed. Secondly, even when it happened, it did not hit the proper targets that we had given. Thirdly, it was almost -- well, you know, it was of little or no consequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were the Muslim soldiers withdrawing from the area denoted by Colonel Karremans as the area that would come under air-strikes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think my answer here would be: I do not know, because I was not in those areas that you are talking about. I don't know whether they withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Muslims ever request to be evacuated from Srebrenica and Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, during my stay there we never received any request from the Muslims to be evacuated from Srebrenica, not any time -- not during meetings, not even when we were discussing at higher levels. No, there's no single time that the Muslims expressed their desire to be removed from the enclave. In other words, the only issue that we got were from the BSA side, saying that the Muslims should leave the enclave, and if they don't, they will remove them from there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the Court please produce P990, marked for identification. P990, marked for identification. Thank you. Here we have it in Serbian and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This was written on 9 July 1995 and sent to the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, personally to Alija Izetbegovic and to Rasim Delic, the general, by the president of Srebrenica municipality, Osman Suljic. Did you know Osman Suljic? Did you have any contacts with him?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, this document is in evidence and not marked for identification. It was received.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see what Mr. Osman Suljic says here. Did you know him or did you hear of him; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here is what he writes to Izetbegovic and Rasim Delic: "Since the aggressor army entered at 1800 hours into the town from the direction of Zeleni Jadar, and our military command is dissolving, as are the members of the 28th Division of the land force, and they are no longer able to do anything to prevent the aggressor forces from entering the town, chaos and panic reign, so it is up to the civilian authorities to make the last unpopular step to save the population. And it is urgent that a meeting be arranged at the highest state and military level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the Serbian aggressor side, with the view to finding a possibility to open a corridor for evacuating the population to the nearest free territory under the control of international organisations. We need an urgent answer, not later than by 2400 hours." My question is: Did you, the UNMOs and the UNPROFOR, know that the Muslim authorities had requested an urgent meeting with the Serbs to arrange the evacuation of their population from Srebrenica already on the 9th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it possible that the Sarajevo Sector headquarters knew or Colonel Karremans -- is it possible they knew about this demand by the civilians from Srebrenica addressed to Alija Izetbegovic and Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be speculation. But also during the meeting that we had with Colonel Karremans, he never mentioned about evacuation requested by the Muslims to this Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We were not aware of that, and it was not mentioned. Evacuation was becoming, obviously, an automatic thing to do, because already the whole place had been bombarded. And as he says in this letter, they are left with no option other than to evacuate the people. And it's during this time that, really, we were looking for alternatives so that we could save a lot of people from further problems. So it is in order. The request, I think, as far as I'm concerned, was okay, though we never got to know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you know that in this period on the 9th, when this letter was written, there was an agreement between the civilian and military authorities on the separation of the population, that they would send to you, to the UNPROFOR, and another part of the population that would go with Becirovic to attempt a breakout? Did you have that information?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the way these things happened is in a way that I don't think there was ever a meeting or people sat down; that is, the Muslim side sat down and discussed and agreed that, You people follow this route, You people follow this route. If there was such an arrangement, it was that automatic response to a situation which was deteriorating by the day, in that those who were able and those who knew, and especially the men, if I may say that, those who knew that if they go towards the BSA side, obviously they'll be eliminated, they had to find their own way out of that problem. Now, for the others, you know, to say that they had agreed that the others relocate to Potocari, that, to me, would be actually -- I would not be able to say that is exactly what happened, because the way they came in from all the villages, it was not like it was pre-planned. Those coming from the Swedish shelter came after their place had really been fully -- almost fully bombarded and taken over by the BSA, so they started streaming into Srebrenica village, itself, thinking that it was safer. Then it became very unsafe. And later on, now they had to go down all the way to Potocari. So I think it was a reaction to an already-existing problem caused by the BSA, that the Muslims had no alternative. In fact, they were left with no alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But that's not what I asked you, whether they did or didn't. I want to discuss your statement again. We need P992, page 6, relating the events of 9 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page is it in English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 6 in English as well, or, rather, 8. We're reading paragraph 9, line 11, in English. And in Serbian, it's page 6, the last paragraph: "From our information, there were no military targets in town."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have the right page, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the previous page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 7 of the paragraph that begins with the date "9 July," which is bolded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I didn't receive --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The mike was not on: "According to our knowledge, there were no military targets in town. I did not understand why they were bombarding the town in such a way, and the only explanation I had is that it was aimed to harass the population to bring them to flee."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And now your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Did you have occasion to see in the town any military from the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He said: "Yes, I saw them."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Could they be a target," was my question. I'm sorry, I had to consult my legal advice.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is just what we saw. And our reports were, I think, about five or so who had uniform, and we reported that we saw them. And, really, for any army, that would not form a lucrative target, where you could use all your artillery, about 250 shells of artillery weapons or in a place just because you want to kill five soldiers. Secondly, some of the targeted areas, like the hospital and the market, really there were no soldiers, as far as we knew. So that is why I discount what you have said, because if you're directing towards that, the five soldiers that we saw, or whatever the numbers, the few soldiers we saw and reported on, that cannot form a lucrative target for any army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether the BiH Army used any targets or any facilities in the city of Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that I can say they had in Srebrenica was the Communications Centre above our PTT building, which was, I think, about a room or one and a half rooms, just small rooms up there with some communication gadgets, VHF radios, just that. There was practically nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And if that room is used to maintain communications with Sarajevo, those who listened in, could they tell that it is just a room and a half, that that is not a command; however, they could still hear the conversation between Becirovic and Izetbegovic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is okay, sir, and what I can add is that before I always conducted, as a general you know this -- before it was conducted, there was a lot of intelligence worked carried out. And when you're hitting a target, you already know the kind of target you're hitting. And if that communication equipment could be confused for a bigger area or a bigger communication equipment or communication centre, maybe that was wrong on the BSA side. But the kind of attack that occurred in that enclave, and especially if I can zero on to Srebrenica town itself, was really more than what could have been necessary to dismantle a communication centre. Secondly, the extent to which the BSA went with their own soldiers on the enclave really needed they needed much more than dismantling that communications centre, because there was no point of bombing the Swedish shelter village, there was no point of bombing the UN compound in Potocari, there was no point in bombarding all the other villages in Srebrenica enclave. Thirdly, and that is maybe the last part of this, the onslaught on Srebrenica was pre-planned, as is evidenced by the reports that we already have and in the meetings that were already there, so -- and they had made their aim very, very clear. They want to remove the Muslims from amongst the Serbs. They want the Serbs to remain there alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Defence and the Trial Chamber what documents are you talking about? Maybe you can show them to us. It seems that you've been quoting and basing your assessments and evaluations on some documents, so could you please show them to us? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you can say which documents you are talking about. If you say a particular, maybe we can request it be shown here. Which one do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You have just said that things had been planned in advance. Are these your assessments, or evaluations, or do you have more specific knowledge and information about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's all documented, and it can be shown. We had meetings, we had -- we had previous meetings with Colonel Vukovic and even Major Nikolic, where they indicated the same, and it's documented in my statement and also in some of the situation reports that we sent. Secondly, it's when Colonel Vukovic said that they do not want Muslim fundamentalists to live in their midst. He's quoted as such, and we wrote it as such. It is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether Vukovic said that he didn't want fundamentalists or Muslims to live in their midst? Do you know if Colonel Vukovic lives in a mixed marriage or not; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may not be in my interest to know. But what I know is that he mentioned that, that Muslims would not be allowed to live amongst the Serbs and that Srebrenica cannot be left to stay with the Muslims. That is well documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You've just told us that a reference was made to fundamentalists. I'm asking you now: Was there any way for you to learn that neither Major Nikolic or Vukovic were either -- not even commanders, but at much lower level in the Bratunac Brigade, and that the only person who had command responsibility in the Bratunac Brigade and who only appeared as an accused at this Tribunal is Blagojevic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we knew was that Colonel Vukovic was a senior officer in the BSA hierarchy, and also Major Nikolic was also a local commander and he represented the interests of the BSA. Thirdly, even when General Ratko Mladic came in, he was accompanied by these senior officers, so he had no reason -- we had no reason at all to doubt that these were senior officers in the BSA hierarchy. And, also, whatever was being passed through Colonel Vukovic and Major Nikolic to us from the BSA side, because we had reason to believe that it was coming from the BSA Command, actually is exactly what happened. So even now, I've got no doubt that they're working for the upper hierarchy. You may not be able to have every general coming to tell you something, but he has these lower people who can be available and can communicate to the relevant people, and that is what Colonel Vukovic and Major Nikolic were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. General Mladic spoke to the Muslims, and he told them that he could choose where to go, any of the four sides of the world. We heard that here. Was his decision more important than Vukovic's or Nikolic's opinion? And the latter two communicated with you -- were in contact with you while you were in Srebrenica, so whose opinion is more important, theirs or General Mladic's opinion?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, General Ratko Mladic's decision and order came -- you know, or request came much later, after what we had discussed with Colonel Vukovic and Major Nikolic. So what came later is what we can take, but we cannot ignore what had been told to us earlier by the two senior officers. And, furthermore, when General Ratko Mladic is talking about this, we need to ask ourselves, when was it, was it before, during, or after the onslaught to the enclave, because if it is coming after the onslaught on the enclave, surely, here these guys had no choice at all other than to get out of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The Trial Chamber here in the Tribunal is best suited to be the judge of that, because they've been privy to all the cases. My question now is this: Did you have a language barrier when you spoke to Nikolic and Vukovic? And if that was the case, who was your interpreter?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, whenever we met with the BSA side, we had Mr. Peter, who was our interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And can we now look at the Serbian language version, page 5, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you move to the next topic, I would like to ask a question to make something more clear. Sir, you answered one question - it is on page 67 - in the following way: "Secondly, it's when Colonel Vukovic said that they do not want Muslim fundamentalists to live in their midst." Then Mr. Tolimir asked you: "Can you please tell us whether Vukovic said that he didn't want fundamentalists or Muslims to live in their midst?" And then your answer was that: "But what I know is that he mentioned that Muslims would not be allowed to live amongst the Serbs." There's a slight change from the words "Muslim fundamentalists" to "Muslims." Did Mr. Vukovic refer to Muslim fundamentalists or to Muslims; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He mentioned both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And he used the word "fundamentalist"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he used the point "fundamentalist," and it's somewhere where it can be gotten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, it's the end of the second session. We must have the second break now, but before we rise, I would like to ask the Registrar to make one additional remark for the record about one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. P85 -- I apologise. P845B and C have been provisionally admitted, pending translation, as two separate exhibits by mistake. P85B -- I'm sorry, P845B is the translation of P845C. Therefore, P845C, 65 ter 3006D, has now been renumbered as P845B, and the former P845B, 65 ter 3006C has been attached as a translation. The number P845C has been erased from the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see agreement from the bench of the Prosecutor. We have to adjourn now, and we'll resume at half past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us continue where we left off. In e-court, page 5 of this statement we're looking at, paragraph 5 in Serbian. And in English kindly show page 7, and then we'll identify the paragraph. It's about the PTT. In English, it's paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will quote to you what you said: "That day, as indicated in the attachments 4 and 5, we indeed had a meeting held in our office at the PTT building, at the request of Chief of Staff Ramiz Becirovic. He requested from Major Franken, deputy commander of DutchBat, to recover the small arms held by DutchBat in order protect themselves. He did not request access to their heavy weapons. He added, according to the notes I have kept, that his forces would refrain from any provocative activities and that they do not intend to fight. He also requested air-strikes." Did you find this passage?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you give these small arms to Ramiz Becirovic that he asked for?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first place, he was not asking us, as observers, to give him the small arms, because they were kept by DutchBat. So it is not us that he was requesting. Secondly, the request was turned down. Therefore, they could not be given the small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he ask for air support instead of heavy weapons? Because it says here he did not request access to heavy weapons, but he did ask for air-strikes. Was that a trade-off?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the way you use the word "trade-off" is not applicable here, in that requesting for air-strikes, there was nothing wrong with that at all, as far as we were concerned, because it was already desperate -- getting desperate in the enclave. And, furthermore, we had already considered about air-strikes, as I mentioned earlier. So it's not an issue of trade-off. Furthermore, trade-off between what and what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I did not ask you what you thought. I am asking about what he thought. He didn't ask for heavy weapons, but he did ask for air-strikes. Which force is greater, air-strikes or heavy weapons, in terms of fire-power? Just tell me your opinion, as observer.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, mine is not exactly an opinion, it's a reality, in that the UN was there to ensure Srebrenica was safe -- to ensure safety, or the people who were inside that enclave. And so when it got to a situation whereby these same people are being bombarded by the BSA from all sides, it was a concern for both the UN and even the people we were to protect inside Srebrenica. So for them to request for air-strikes, really, there was nothing wrong with that. They are not the ones who are coming to make the air-strikes. If it was for the heavy weapons, they're the ones to use the heavy weapons. But at this time it is the air-strikes from the UN aircraft. Secondly, you asked about the fire-power of aircraft and heavy weapons. It depends on what type of aircraft and what type of ground -- that is, artillery power. So as far as I am concerned, the aircraft have got heavier fire-power, but I said it depends on -- I dare to say you cannot compare directly just like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you convey Ramiz's request to your command, the request for air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may say it a second time, we, as observers, had already considered that; not the request from the Muslim side, but the need for air-strikes against the BSA positions. So we didn't need to be probed by anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does that mean that your reports do not reflect what Ramiz said at that meeting to you, to the other people who were there at the meeting in the PTT building? You can tell me which day it was. Was it the 6th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- I can't remember what was put in the situation reports, but at least these requests, we got it, and I think we conveyed to the higher headquarters. But I'm not sure which report we put it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see here that the PTT could arguably be a target if meetings are held there with Muslims and there are meetings held there and there are also premises of the various organisations. Could the PTT be a military target?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the PTT could not have formed a lucrative target for the BSA. But according to the way they were bombarding the place, any place -- anything was, to them, a target, and that is why they were bombarding everywhere else, including the market, including the hospital, including the villages. So anything to them was -- as far as we were concerned, was a target. They wanted to destroy the whole place. Secondly, the fact that we were holding meetings there, actually, should have informed them not to target that particular building, because they know UN personnel are also in those areas. They are holding meetings with the Muslims, with an aim of ensuring that the situation does not deteriorate. And even some of those meetings, obviously, we were conveying issues given to us by the BSA in meetings with them, so they knew that we were going to hold meetings with the BSA, so they didn't have to target that particular building, well knowing very well UNMOs who are staying there. Secondly, we would hold meetings, unless they wanted us to be target and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since the post office, in your view, is not a military target, and we will look at all kinds of military targets in another area, tell me, how is it possible that three years later, in the aggression of NATO against Yugoslavia, the television building was proclaimed to be a military target by NATO and a large number of civilians was killed? How come that the post office is not a military target, because it serves as a hub of communication between the military command in Srebrenica and the command in Sarajevo? Following your logic, could I say that all the casualties in Iran, in Afghanistan, in all the theatres of war, were planned by the Muslims, because you stated a moment ago that Serbs pre-planned everything? Could that logic be applied, then, to NATO?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reasoning I have, and the one I've already used, is that considering the fire-power that was used there and the targets which were being aimed at by the Bosnian Serb Army, it's difficult to tell whether they were targeting that building just because of the communication equipment which were there. You talked about a television -- television equipment in Afghanistan and all that, but for sure that kind of bombardment did not -- was not warranted, and especially considering the situation in the whole of that enclave, that these people did not have the arms and they actually were not even resisting. The resistance that was there was actually minimal. So, really, the point of bombarding heavily that particular place was not warranted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: How many days did they resist, and did the UNPROFOR help them resist?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, what I can say is that I don't think the UNPROFOR was there to help the Muslims resist the attack from the BSA. Secondly, they tried to resist for some time, but, of course, they did not have the fire-power that the BSA had. So it was a resistance that was a difficult world. And they give in after, I think, four days -- two, three, or four days or so, and that is the time the enclave fell. And the rest is well documented.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see P957 [Realtime transcript read in error "P977"]. That refers to military targets and the post office. And then we will come back to the issue you just mentioned, the Muslim resistance and the support of the UNPROFOR in that, if any. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We now see a document sent by the Defence Ministry, the Defence Ministry's section in Srebrenica, on 22nd February 1995, to the Secretariat of Defence in Tuzla, and it says: "Subject: Overview of business premises used by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina." It refers to the premises used by the military forces in Srebrenica. Could you please bring back the previous document so the witness can follow. I'm repeating for the record. This is a document from the Department of Defence in the municipality of Srebrenica, sent on the 22nd February 1995 to the secretariat in Tuzla, where they report which premises in town they're using for the purposes of the army. And they say: "In accordance with your document, we hereby send you a list of office space used by the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the territory of Srebrenica municipality." I'll just indicate a few buildings in Srebrenica and in Potocari, because you spoke mostly about the shelling of Srebrenica and Potocari. This is old town Srebrenica: "Lovac feature." Then: "Command of the 8th Operative Group, Srebrenica." And C: "UPI Enterprise, Srebrenica. "D. Total area covers 275 square metres, and the whole area is used." And then the next one says: "Future is used as command's command base." And, second: "All headquarters of the Territorial Defence ..." Then let's move to Potocari: "280th Mountain Brigade is using a family home owned by Meho Hrvacic in Potocari." Another family home, another family house. And then you say you can't understand why they targeted Potocari and Srebrenica when there were no military targets there. Can you see, from this document, that there were military targets in Srebrenica and Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the record, there was a minor mistake with the number in the transcript, although Mr. Tolimir has indicated the right number. On page 75, line 15, it is said "P977," but, in fact, it is P957, what we are looking at. And now Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The list is self-explanatory. I've never seen it before. This is the first time I'm seeing it. Secondly, even the way he's explained, like in Srebrenica, itself, we have the operations room, which was actually a communications centre, but I still maintain what I said earlier, in that some of these targets really, according to my own assessment, according to how I would operate as a military person, these would not form a basis of bombarding the whole place and actually shelling it throughout to finish the whole enclave. It won't, it won't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was this document shown to you in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may have been shown. I'm not very sure. I can't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Before testifying here, did you review all the documents you had the Popovic case? I think the Prosecutor asked you the same thing in direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I reviewed all of them. And I would like to add, because you're asking questions on the same issues, these ones, that is, the communication area in PTT building, compare it -- being a military person, compare it with a unit, that is, a battalion, and then see the difference that I'm actually talking about, in that this, to me, does not even come to even a section. There may be a section, yeah, a section plus, a company -- no, not even a company; it cannot. And for a whole army to come and combat and bombard a place because of a few communication gadgets, as far as I knew about them, because I saw that place, I have been up there, to me it did not make that much sense. Secondly, if you hear of a command or a headquarter being in a certain family house, really, what are we talking about? A family house? What would be there in such a headquarter? We're talking maybe, if there's anything, just a few people, maybe two, three, four, five, or something like that. Does that warrant these kind of bombardment? Those are some of the questions we need to ask ourselves, instead of just targeting the areas which are listed as headquarters. Headquarters of what? What are the number of people who could be expected in that particular house at any moment? What kind of equipment would be there? Then compare with a regular army, with a battalion, surely. And these, the BSA, were not even their own battalion, because they had the support of all the heavy weapons. It was more than a brigade. So because of the heavy weapons that they had, they had tanks, more than a troop of, you know, tanks, artillery. You know, it was heavy, a lot of it. Everything -- they had everything. And you cannot compare that organisation, that equipping, with what you are showing us here. I know it is very difficult to understand some of these things, but it is not fathomable, you know, to equate something like this. The feature, you know, if I got the feature of the Territorial Defence Staff of Srebrenica, how many soldiers were in Srebrenica, itself? Very few, if any, very few. You know, the reason why -- if you allow me just to explain a bit. If you go to the BSA side, they had everything. Okay, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I am aware of your position and your opinion, as presented in this court, but I asked you about something entirely different, and that's why we'll move on. You said a moment ago that the Muslims were putting up resistance. Now, I'll read to you from the transcript of evidence given by members of the UNPROFOR, who stated -- testified they participated in the war on the Muslim side. Page 3475, lines 7 and 8, evidence given by Mr. Franken on 9 July. He says: "I said it earlier. We were in a state of war with the VRS, and we opened fire together with the Muslim Army." You can check that on the transcript. It's on the left side. You can check it. And if it's not, can it be shown to the witness? Further on, when the Defence asked: "Was it your mandate to destroy the weapons of the VRS and go to war with the VRS after the green order." The response on page 3484, he said: "No, it was not within our mandate. Still, my mandate changed significantly from the moment when the UN ordered me to defend Srebrenica, and that was the reason why I gave the green order to that effect." Now, based on what I just put to you, since Major Franken commanded UNPROFOR forces in Srebrenica in the absence of Karremans, does his evidence about the green order and that he was in war -- at war with the VRS run counter to the evidence you gave here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We'll have that part of the transcript on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Not yet, but it will come up immediately. Mr. Tolimir was referring to page 3475, lines 8 and 7. 3475. But, in fact, it is line 8 and the next lines. Sir, do you see that part? It is now marked in yellow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you firstly comment on this first part, and then you will be shown the other part of that answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I can comment and say that this was given by -- if it is -- because I've never seen this -- is given by Major Franken, as we have been told, and if they decided to fight together with the Muslims, that was not communicated to us. We were not privy to this information. And, secondly, I don't think it was in their mandate, but at least they had a mandate to protect the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let's see page 3484. Mr. Tolimir, which line are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's lines 1 and 2. On 3483, it's line 25, and up to page 3484, line 3 or 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the witness has the opportunity to read that part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the one who was answering this question has answered everything. They said the mandate changed and they were ordered to do something, and they continued to do it. So I don't see now the question I should answer there. It's so answered. There was a change in mandate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you aware that the UNPROFOR and the Muslims acted together against the VRS and VRS targets, beginning with the 5th of July, as evidenced by the testimony of certain witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Once again, Mr. President -- pardon the frog in my throat. If we could have a citation, which witnesses he's talking about when he refers to the 5th of July as evidenced by the testimony of certain witnesses. Again, we have no problem with cross-examination, General Tolimir pursuing whatever line he wants, but we just want to know what the basis is for this question that he's putting to the witness, if he's going to be referring to certain witnesses. And, again, I just want to refer back to some prior questions. There was a line of questions about private testimony that was before the Trial Chamber, and again we don't want to restrict General Tolimir's testimony. If he can just give us, for example, the PW numbers of those witnesses, we've got no problem with him putting questions. I understand we don't want to put the names, but I just want our position to be clear. We don't want to cut off that cross-examination. We just want to know what the basis is, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, can you help the Chamber and the Prosecution with more detailed information?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Thayer. This was said by a witness who was an UNPROFOR commander, and he said "beginning with the 5th," and that was in corroboration with Franken's evidence. I agree with that. He was confirming Franken's testimony, and he said "the 5th." I think Mr. Thayer will remember who he was, and we can see that from the transcript of his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please tell us the name of this witness. We have heard lots of witnesses, and we would like to know the name, if you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Nicolai.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And where do we find that part in the transcript of his testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My adviser will find it and give you a reference while we continue working. I do not speak English. I'm working from my memory. I think I remember he said the 5th. It's in the transcript. Whether he was mistaken or not, I really don't know. I can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When was the green order given, if he knows? When was it given, and when did it come into force?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not aware of a green order, whether it was given or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I understand the answer. Regardless of the answer, my assistant will find these references and provide them to the OTP and the Trial Chamber. The witness doesn't need them, because he doesn't know about the order anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said here, in your statement, that a helicopter crashed. You said you heard about it and then you saw it, and Ramiz Becirovic was somehow involved. Can you tell the Trial Chamber all that you know about this incident? And if you can't find it, I'll -- and if you can't remember, I'll find it in your statement and quote. You said it on page 4 of your statement, paragraph 6, lines 1 through 7. That was in Serbian. Sorry, in Serbian, that's page 4, paragraph 6, lines 1 through 7; P992. Can it be shown to the witness, if necessary? If not, the witness can just answer. In English, it's page 4, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's on the screen now. And what is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is -- perhaps the Prosecutor should have the floor first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Tolimir -- [Overlapping speakers] I think Mr. Tolimir is expecting that Mr. Thayer knows exactly to which part of the document he's referring.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If it's the portion referring to the helicopter crashing, which Colonel Kingori has testified about already, it's two pages from this one, page 4 of the document, itself; page 6, I guess, of e-court. So if we just go forward two pages, it's the fourth paragraph down, I believe. There it is, the sentence: "Once he called for a meeting ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You've already read it. I don't need to quote. Colonel Vukovic had told you that a helicopter crashed and what happened happened, and you said you later heard it from the people, and you later saw Becirovic injured. Can you tell us if you reported to your superiors about it, and did you make inquiries about what this helicopter flight was all about?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we reported about all this. After we were informed by Colonel Vukovic and got to know that Ramiz was injured, we realised, actually, a helicopter must have crashed, and we conveyed this to our headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware that the Muslims were arming themselves by air-lifts, using helicopters, at the time when this helicopter crashed, and that the command in Srebrenica kept in touch with the command in Tuzla, and that they went on command reconnaissance together?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were not aware. But Colonel Vukovic and, I think, Major Nikolic brought these issues to us, and we started the investigations so that we could convey the same with a bit of certainty. But we could not be able to get to know whether it was true. There was re-arming going on of the Muslim side. We could not for sure know whether it was happening, because we never witnessed any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir and all others, we have to adjourn now for the week. I'm very sorry, Witness. The cross-examination hasn't finished, and the Prosecution has certainly the opportunity for re-examination, so that it is necessary that you come back on Monday for the continuation of your examination. Have you any idea, Mr. Tolimir, about the remaining time for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We will finish the cross-examination within the first session of the first following day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is encouraging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was just told that your expectation was to be able to leave today, but it is not possible, and we can't sit a longer time today because of other commitments, so that there is no other option as to continue your examination on Monday. I'm very sorry for that. On Monday, in the afternoon, 2.15. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 20th day of September, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.16 p.m.,
